Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Non-binary
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Special Education Teacher
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Vignette:
Kai is a 27-year-old special education teacher who works in a public elementary school, supporting children with behavioral and emotional challenges. They live with their partner, Sam, in a small apartment near the coast. The trauma that fractured their sense of safety began about fourteen months ago, when a former student’s parent started appearing at the school parking lot, waiting by Kai’s car. At first it was just a few times, and Kai tried to dismiss it as coincidence. But then the parent began following them after work—driving slowly behind Kai’s car for several blocks, pulling over when Kai pulled over, and once, standing at the far end of their street just before dusk. The worst moment came on a Tuesday evening in late fall. Kai had stayed late to finish lesson plans. As they walked to the car, they heard footsteps—steady, deliberate, behind them but never close enough to see a face. They quickened their pace; the footsteps quickened too. When they finally turned around, the parent was standing motionless under a broken streetlight, just watching. Kai ran to the car, locked the doors, and drove home shaking. The police were called, a no-contact order was filed, and the parent eventually stopped appearing. But for Kai, the world never felt the same.

In the weeks that followed, Kai’s memory of that evening refused to settle into a coherent story. Some parts were hyper-clear—the sound of gravel underfoot, the orange glow of the streetlight, the weight of the car key pressed between their fingers. Other parts were gaps, like a film with frames cut out. They could not remember unlocking the car door, only that they were suddenly inside it. They could not recall what the parent had been wearing, only the stillness of that silhouette. The memory came in disconnected fragments that did not fit together, leaving Kai with an incomplete picture that felt more unsettling than full recall would have been. They began to wonder if they had missed something, if there was a warning sign they should have caught. Night after night, Kai lay awake mentally replaying the weeks before the incident, scanning every interaction with the parent for clues of what they could have done differently—a different route home, a different time to leave, a different parking spot. This rumination became a nightly ritual, a way of trying to solve a puzzle that had no solution.

Day by day, Kai’s body remained on alert. At work, in the classroom, they found themselves scanning the hallway through the door’s small window, checking the faces of every adult who passed. The sound of footsteps in the corridor, even the brisk steps of a colleague, made Kai’s stomach drop. They had learned to position their desk so they could see the door at all times, and they left the classroom blinds open so no movement outside went unseen. At home, they could not relax. Sitting on the couch felt dangerous; closing their eyes in the shower felt like inviting a threat. Kai had come to believe that if they let their guard down for even a moment, something bad would happen again—and next time, they might not get away. So they kept moving, kept checking, kept listening. They stopped taking walks after dark, stopped going to the grocery store alone, and began taking a longer, more open route to work even though it cost them twenty extra minutes. Their partner, Sam, noticed that Kai flinched whenever Sam came up behind them or made a sudden movement in the kitchen. Kai knew this was straining their relationship, but they could not stop themselves from reacting; the surge of adrenaline was automatic, and it felt necessary.

The classroom itself became the most difficult setting. Kai was known for being calm and patient with their students, but now they found themselves distracted during lessons, their attention pulled toward the door or the windows. They had started carrying a small pocket-sized whistle on their keychain, an object of preparation they told no one about. They never used it, but its presence allowed them to feel slightly less exposed. Last month, a delivery person knocked on the classroom door and then stepped inside without waiting for a response. The sudden movement—a person entering the space Kai had been trying so hard to control—made Kai shout, startling the children. They later apologized, but the incident left them shaken and ashamed. It was that moment—seeing the worried faces of their students, feeling the loss of composure in the one place they had always felt competent—that finally pushed Kai to seek help. They made an appointment with a therapist who specialized in trauma. Now, sitting in the waiting room, Kai is afraid that talking about the stalking will make the fragments of memory worse, that digging into the gaps will open a hole they cannot climb out of. But they are also afraid of staying this way: always scanning, always listening, never able to let go of the feeling that someone is still behind them, just out of sight.
